report.tagline: The iPhone, Apple's main product and the centre of an ecosystem of devices and paid services, compared with Vision Pro, Apple's costly attempt at a new category.
report.simpleSummary: Apple sells premium devices, and the iPhone is the heart of it: about half of Apple's revenue. Once you own an iPhone, your photos, messages, apps and payments all live in Apple's world, and it works best with an Apple Watch, AirPods and Mac, so people rarely switch. Apple then earns more every month from services like iCloud, the App Store and Apple Music. Vision Pro, a $3,499 headset launched in 2024, shows the other side: great technology that most people did not yet need or could not afford, so it sold far less than the iPhone ever did.

overview.whatItDoes: Apple designs iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch, AirPods and Vision Pro, plus the software (iOS, macOS, visionOS) and services that run on them. The iPhone is sold through Apple Stores, carriers and resellers worldwide, including India where Apple now makes many iPhones. Vision Pro is a mixed-reality headset that places apps and video around you, controlled by eyes, hands and voice; it got an M5 chip update in 2025 but remains a niche product.
howItWorks: Apple sells premium hardware at high prices and high margins, with a new iPhone every September.
Each device signs in to one Apple Account, linking iCloud, iMessage, FaceTime, Apple Pay and the App Store.
Devices work together: AirDrop, Handoff, Watch unlock, AirPods switching, iPhone mirroring on Mac.
Services earn monthly revenue from the installed base: iCloud storage, Apple Music, TV+, Arcade, AppleCare and a share of App Store sales.
Trade-ins and monthly instalment plans make upgrading easier.
Vision Pro tried to start a new platform, spatial computing, with its own apps and the same Apple Account.
overview.valueProposition: Devices that are simple, private and work together, with long software support and resale value. For Vision Pro: a personal cinema and infinite screens anywhere, at a very high price.

businessModel.summary: Apple makes most money selling premium hardware, led by the iPhone, and growing money from services sold to people who already own its devices. Services have much higher margins than hardware.

revenueStreams.detail: $209.6 billion in fiscal 2025, about half of revenue.
$109.2 billion in fiscal 2025: App Store, iCloud, Music, TV+, AppleCare, Apple Pay and Google search payments.
iPad $28 billion in fiscal 2025; Mac also tens of billions.
$35.7 billion in fiscal 2025, including Watch, AirPods and Vision Pro; down 3.6%.

businessModel.pricing: iPhone 17 range in the US starts around $799; Pro models higher. In India, iPhones start around ₹70,000 to ₹80,000 for the base model. Vision Pro: $3,499. Services from $0.99 a month (iCloud 50 GB) to Apple One bundles.
costDrivers: Components and assembly, mostly in China, India and Vietnam
R&D on chips, software and new categories like Vision Pro
businessModel.unitEconomics: On an $800 iPhone, Apple's hardware gross margin is roughly 35% to 40%, so it keeps about $300 before R&D and marketing. Then that iPhone owner may spend $10 to $20 a month on services like iCloud, Music and App Store purchases, where margins are around 70%. Over a four-year life, services can add several hundred dollars of high-margin revenue. Vision Pro is the opposite: high component costs, low volume and few services, so it likely makes little or no profit and is a long-term bet.

howTheyGetUsers: Switching campaigns and Move to iOS tools
Expansion in India with local manufacturing and Apple Stores
whatBringsUsersBack: Ecosystem lock-in: data, apps and devices tied to one account
growth.moat: Apple's moat is the ecosystem. Once your photos, messages, apps, Watch and AirPods are tied to an Apple Account, switching to Android means losing convenience and money. Add a premium brand and custom chips, and the iPhone is extremely hard to beat. Vision Pro shows the limit: the moat helps sell a new product, but it cannot create demand if the product is too expensive or not useful enough yet.

pmLessons: An ecosystem is the strongest moat: each product makes the others more valuable.
Hardware sells once; services sell every month. Grow both.
A new category needs a clear use case and a reachable price. Great technology is not enough, as Vision Pro shows.
Even a giant can be late; Apple's AI gap shows the cost of waiting too long.

interviewQuestions.question: Why did Vision Pro not take off like the iPhone?
interviewQuestions.hint: Price, comfort, few apps, unclear daily use case; compare with iPhone's clear jobs (phone, internet, iPod).

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow iPhone share in India?
interviewQuestions.hint: Affordability (EMI, refurbished, older models), local manufacturing, retail, local features.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Apple's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Ecosystem depth or active devices per user, linked to retention and services revenue.

interviewQuestions.question: The EU forces Apple to allow other app stores. What would you do as an App Store PM?
interviewQuestions.hint: Protect users with security, compete on trust and convenience, adjust fees, track developer and user retention.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature to get more iPhone users to buy an Apple Watch.
interviewQuestions.hint: Find the job (health, fitness, safety), show value in iPhone, trial or bundles, measure attach rate.
